newsitem.title: FINLAND: World's mutual insurers face harsher times.
newsitem.headline: World's mutual insurers face harsher times.

text.p: Mutual insurers face a declining market share, problems in providing sufficient capital to meet solvency requirements and increased competition from joint stock companies, more than 130 delegates at an industry conference were told last week.

AISAM (Association Internationale des Societes d'Assurance Mutuelle) president Emile Aldeweireldt, chief executive officer of Belgian insurer APRA, said a wave of demutualisations was occurring worldwide.
However, mutuals were still a major part of the insurance industry and include international groups such as AXA.

Mutual life companies in 1994 had market share of 89 percent in Japan, 71 percent in Australia, 57 percent in the U.S. and 53 percent in Canada. In Finland, non-life mutuals held a share of 38 percent and life companies 62 percent, Aldeweireldt said.
During the conference, AXA's way of growing into an international group was presented as one example of mutuals could overcome limitations.

Hanns-Juergen Weigel of Alte Leipziger said,"the principle of mutuality can only survive if the benchmark of shareholder value, as advocated by joint stock companies, is answered with another benchmark by mutual insurers. This benchmark must be the concept of member value."
The structure of mutuals and their difference from joint stock companies should be made part of the marketing strategy, he added.
Rodrigo Donoso Silva, president of Chilean insurer Mutual de Seguridad, Camara Chilena de la Construccion, highlighted the role of mutuals in Chilean workers compensation insurance.

Larry Forrester, president of the U.S. mutuals association NAMIC (National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies), said that the U.S. property and casualty market would undergo significant change within the next three to five years.

"To date, we have not seen a rush to demutualise," he said. "However, many observers predict the mutual insurance industry will undergo the same demutualisation that the mutual savings and loan industry experienced in the 70s and 80s."

He warned that a demutualised company would change in outlook and culture. In workshops, delegates discussed new methods of acquiring sufficient funds to keep mutuals' capital and thus solvency in line with legal requirements and business expansion in view of the fact that they cannot easily tap capital markets.
Other workshops dealt with the role of members and the difference to joint stock companies.

During the funding workshop, several delegates warned that plans to rearrange solvency requirements under European Union directives would mean a threat to small mutuals which operate on a regional basis or for certain professions and which were were "very healthy".
Delegates said they were especially concerned that the proposed higher requirements for guarantee funds would hit these insurers.
AISAM has 212 member companies in 27 countries.
